@C_Barraud's Wednesday Brief is packed with analysis of the Democrats winning control of the House and Senate which, in contrast to conventional thinking, is seeing both bonds and stocks (and gold) higher with the asset taking the biggest hit the dollar.

▪️ Dollar: Bloomberg’s dollar index fell as much as 0.5%, its biggest drop in two months, to its lowest since late September. The Swiss franc, yen and euro all gained.
▪️ Treasuries: the 10-year yield is down 3 basis points to 4.93%. The 5-year fell as much as 9 basis points to 4.67% before pairing some gains.
▪️ Stocks: S&P 500 futures recovered from a 1.4% overnight drop to trade about 0.9% higher, and Nasdaq 100 futures erased a 2.4% slide.
▪️ Gold is up nearly 3% since Tuesday’s close.

Why bonds are rallying: Wellington’s Brij Khurana told Bloomberg divided government has historically been good for Treasuries, since a Democratic Congress limits Trump’s room for more tax cuts and spending that would need more issuance. 
Nedgroup’s David Roberts added a growth angle: Democratic control could slow the AI buildout that has been driving growth and inflation, so the Fed might not need to hike next year.

Why the dollar fell hardest: its 4% rally since early September was built on the AI boom, through money pouring into US tech and AI-driven inflation lifting Fed hike bets. Democrats are talking tougher tech rules and higher taxes on companies and high earners. Crédit Agricole’s David Forrester said the dollar’s “Achilles’ heel” is being exposed. Nomura’s Dominic Bunning added that investors were leaning long the dollar, so there’s room for those bets to unwind.

Vontobel’s Andrew Jackson though noted that blocking new spending doesn’t shrink the existing deficit, so heavy issuance could limit how far long yields fall. Ed Yardeni warned a Democratic sweep could make debt ceiling talks messy, with shutdown risk that could push yields higher (although Republicans may look to get the debt ceiling taken care of in the lame duck session). And dollar bulls have oil: Bloomberg notes the dollar’s gains could resume if Middle East turbulence lifts crude and Fed hike bets.

What to watch: the Treasury’s refunding announcement later this morning, where dealers expect groundwork for possible 2027 cuts to the longest-dated auctions, offset by more bills and shorter notes (Commerzbank expects no coupon changes for now).

In the third-quarter Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS), banks reported that business loan demand weakened for the first time since the second quarter of 2025. But other data doesn’t show businesses borrowing less.

The Fed’s weekly bank lending data shows commercial & industrial (C&I) loans are up 11.3% year-over-year, the fastest since early 2023 (h/t Ed Yardeni), and we know equipment spending surged at a 20.9% annualized rate in third-quarter GDP.

The banks’ own explanation hints at what’s going on: “customer borrowing shifting to more attractive bank or nonbank funding sources.”

Worth noting, the survey’s demand reading has historically led actual C&I loan growth by about three quarters (correlation of 0.64 since 1991), so either loan growth cools into mid-2027 or the survey is off this time.

Interestingly, though, while banks left business loan standards little changed, they tightened standards on every type of loan to the nonbank lenders (nondepository financial institutions, or NDFIs) that may be taking their business:

▪️ Private credit (business credit intermediaries): a net 22% of banks tightened, while a net 10.7% saw stronger demand from them
▪️ Private equity funds: 15.4% tightened, demand up 5.4%
▪️ Mortgage and consumer credit intermediaries and other NDFIs: 16.7% to 20.4% tightened
Despite that, bank loans to NDFIs are up 20.3% year-over-year, about the 20% to 22% pace they’ve held all year. Meanwhile, loan-loss reserves are flat at $202 billion while total loans grew 7.9%, so coverage slipped to 1.42% of loans from 1.54% a year ago.

Some other nuggets from the SLOOS report:
▪️ Commercial real estate standards tightened in all three categories for the first time since the third quarter of 2024, with large banks flipping tighter after six straight surveys of easing on construction and multifamily loans
▪️ Mortgage demand weakened in all seven categories, while credit card demand was the strongest since the third quarter of 2022

I have not used technical analysis much in analyzing bond yields, but I've been hearing more and more of it so thought this Reuters article via @C_Barraud was interesting on the 10-year Treasury yield. 

It notes the yield had fallen four straight weeks through Friday to 4.91%, down from a 24-year intraday high of 5.36% on Oct. 7. It was 3.96% just before the Iran war began.

Reuters says it’s “too soon to say the rising trend that began with the Iran war is over.”

The key line they say is the rising 20-week moving average near 4.81%, which has halted pullbacks several times this year. Analysts aren’t likely to treat the slide as durable until the 10-year breaks below it and stays there.

If it breaks, support levels are:
▪ 4.75% to 4.68%
▪ ~4.62%
▪ 4.50% to 4.40%, the top of a symmetrical triangle, which also holds the 20-month moving average

If yields turn back up, resistance levels are:
▪ ~5.07%, the upper yearly Bollinger Band
▪ 5.16% to 5.18%
▪ 5.3645%, the Oct. 7 peak
▪ 5.48% to 5.52%, then the 50-year moving average near 5.65%

A move above 6% would bring 6.24% into view. That’s a Fibonacci retracement of the 1981 to 2020 decline in yields.

Similarly, a sharp decline indicates a reduction in risk appetite, and at extreme levels it can indicate that markets may have overshot. RAI signals are most powerful when the level of risk appetite is very low below -1.5, with levels closer to -2.0 giving the clearest signal over longer time horizons, as at such levels the asymmetry of subsequent medium term equity return becomes very positively skewed. September JOLTS strong across the board: openings rise the most since May, hires up the most since March, quits the most since May 2023, and layoffs the least since March 2025.

▪️ Openings: up 333,000 to 7.52 million, the highest since May, beating the 7.10 million consensus by more than 400,000 (August revised up 111,000). There were 1.06 openings per unemployed worker, above 1.0 for a sixth straight month.
▪️ Hires: up 131,000 to 5.40 million, the highest since March, with the hires rate at 3.4%. Hires minus separations, an employment proxy, was 83,000, against a 29,000 gain in September payrolls.
▪️ Quits: up 321,000, the most since May 2023, to 3.37 million, the highest since March 2025, and the quits rate rose to 2.1% from 1.9%. Accommodation and food services accounted for 197,000 of it; excluding that though industry quits still rose 124,000 the most since March 2025
▪️ Layoffs: down 127,000 to 1.64 million, the lowest since March 2025, with the rate at 1.0%. The catch: August was revised up 127,000, turning its reported decline into a 66,000 increase.

Revisions also undid two of last month’s stories. The August drop in openings at the smallest firms shrank to 152,000 from 335,000, and August private-sector hires now show a 76,000 gain rather than a decline.

Fits Fed Chair Warsh’s “quite positive” read on employment. It also gives the hawks more firepower although a lot more data before the December 8-9 meeting.

US Construction Spending (M/M) Sep: -1.9% (est 0.6%; prev 0.9%; prev R 2.0%)

September construction spending saw the biggest drop since April 2020, but the details matter.

The drop came almost entirely from Census’s implied home improvement (remodeling) figure, which fell a record 13% (data back to 1993). That $49B decline was larger than the entire drop in private construction. Excluding remodeling, spending rose 0.4%, and with August revised up to +2.0%, spending is about flat versus July.

▪️ Don’t count on a reversion: big remodeling drops rebounded the next month 19 of 22 times from 1993 to 2002, but only 1 of 4 times since
▪️ But a revision is more likely: the first estimate has been revised by 2.3 points on average since 2023, and the direction flipped in a third of months
▪️ Data centers hit another record at $96.5B, +90% y/y, their 10th straight monthly gain and now 4.4% of all construction
▪️ Electric power also set a record at $146.9B
▪️ In Q3, data centers (+$21.9B) and power (+$10.4B) added more than the entire quarterly gain (+$24.5B), as everything else in private nonresidential has been mostly flat since January
▪️ GDP: private nonresidential came in $8.6B above what BEA assumed for Q3, pointing to about a 0.1-point upward revision. The remodeling drop doesn’t feed GDP directly, because BEA uses its own improvements estimate

Watch whether the remodeling drop gets revised away in the December 1 report.

Traders Sell China's Latest Effort to Put a Floor Under Markets

A little under the radar, China’s benchmark CSI 300 equity index fell 8.5% in October, its worst month since January 2016 (−21.0%), narrowly beating the October 2018 (−8.3%) at the height of the trade war. It also fell for a record 12 straight weeks through Friday, per Bloomberg. The index is down 15% this year.

As @C_Barraud notes in his Tuesday Brief this happened despite state-fund buying since July and earlier curbs on share sales. So Beijing returned to the toolbox Monday:

▪️ The PBOC cut the rate on its buyback/stake-increase relending facility to 1% from 1.25% and made it permanent. About 440 billion yuan of those loans have been contracted, with more than 280 billion disbursed.
▪️ It is restarting the swap facility that lets brokers, funds and insurers swap assets for liquidity to buy stocks. 31 firms are approved and have applied for more than 100 billion yuan of quotas. Operations start in the coming days (outstanding balance is 105 billion).
▪️ The CSRC will make buybacks easier, including when shares trade below their IPO price, and is studying looser margin-financing rules.
▪️ Per the FT, regulators gave banks “window guidance” to pause IPOs and suspended large share sales by existing holders until markets recover.
▪️ Bloomberg says turnover in national-team-favored ETFs jumped to 120 billion yuan, the highest since late January, which suggests the state stepped in directly.

The market was less than impressed. The tech-heavy Star 50 fell 3.8% on Tuesday, wiping out Monday’s anticipation rally. The CSI 300 was down as much as 1.2% before closing down 0.2%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.6%.

Why it isn’t working: these are the September 2024 tools without the September 2024 punch. Back then the facilities came with rate cuts, and the CSI 300 jumped about 21% in a single month. This time there is no rate cut, and as one Shanghai CIO told Bloomberg, the tools have been around for two years and add no new support. Capital Economics says a lasting turnaround needs earnings growth, which near term means monetary or fiscal support.

History on IPO freezes isn’t encouraging either. Beijing halted listings in early July 2015, and the CSI 300 still fell 14.7% that month and another 11.8% in August before it found a floor.

What to watch: whether the PBOC adds a policy-rate or reserve-requirement cut (the missing piece compared with 2024), how fast the swap quotas are drawn down, and whether national-team ETF volume stays elevated.

▪️ The PBOC cut the rate on its buyback/stake-increase relending facility to 1% from 1.25% and made it permanent. About 440 billion yuan of those loans have been contracted, with more than 280 billion disbursed.
▪️ It is restarting the swap facility that lets brokers, funds and insurers swap assets for liquidity to buy stocks. 31 firms are approved and have applied for more than 100 billion yuan of quotas. Operations start in the coming days (outstanding balance is 105 billion).
▪️ The CSRC will make buybacks easier, including when shares trade below their IPO price, and is studying looser margin-financing rules.
▪️ Per the FT, regulators gave banks “window guidance” to pause IPOs and suspended large share sales by existing holders until markets recover.
▪️ Bloomberg says turnover in national-team-favored ETFs jumped to 120 billion yuan, the highest since late January, which suggests the state stepped in directly.

The market was less than impressed. The tech-heavy Star 50 fell 3.8% on Tuesday, wiping out Monday’s anticipation rally. The CSI 300 was down as much as 1.2% before closing down 0.2%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.6%.

Why it isn’t working: these are the September 2024 tools without the September 2024 punch. Back then the facilities came with rate cuts, and the CSI 300 jumped about 21% in a single month. This time there is no rate cut, and as one Shanghai CIO told Bloomberg, the tools have been around for two years and add no new support. Capital Economics says a lasting turnaround needs earnings growth, which near term means monetary or fiscal support.

History on IPO freezes isn’t encouraging either. Beijing halted listings in early July 2015, and the CSI 300 still fell 14.7% that month and another 11.8% in August before it found a floor.

What to watch: whether the PBOC adds a policy-rate or reserve-requirement cut (the missing piece compared with 2024), how fast the swap quotas are drawn down, and whether national-team ETF volume stays elevated.
